newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela to continue gold opening despite protest.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela to continue gold opening despite protest.

text.p: The Venezuelan government said Wednesday it would continue with plans to open a huge forest reserve in eastern Venezuela to gold mining, despite a growing wave of protests by environmental and Indian groups.

The Imataca tropical forest reserve, which covers an area the size of El Salvador near the Guyanese border, has become the focal point of heated argument after the government recently moved to legalize gold mining there.
"The Venezuelan government is going to continue with its policy of rescuing Imataca," information minister Fernando Egana told reporters.

Government officials argue the forest's delicate ecosystem is already being destroyed by some 20,000 illegal foreign miners working gold reserves valued at $150 billion dollars. Better, the government says, to open the area to rational and clean exploitation rather than let the current disorder prevail.

"Imataca has been abandoned for years and the subject of every type of degradation," Egana said. "Essentially, ecocide was happening, and because of that, the government decided to pass the mining decree."
The Army has added that currently it cannot "guarantee defense of the country's sovereignty or the environment," in the remote region.

But environmentalists, civil groups, academics and politicians from across the political spectrum say the proposed law only turns over the mining to foreign multinationals, who will leave the forest ruined.
According to Wednesday press reports, local Indian groups who the government claim back the initiative also say they have been manipulated and that the government cannot count on their support.

Ministers say that deforestation has already become a problem in the forest, as has poisoning from mercury, and disease and prostitution in improvised mining settlements. ((-- Omar Lugo, Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
